A wrong turn doesn't feel like anything in the moment. It feels like you're lost.

Kevin got lost before GPS existed, in an area he didn't know, and pulled into a gas station for directions. A brand new Ferrari pulled up behind him. The man driving it turned out to be a local billionaire — someone he'd heard of but never met. One wrong turn later, they were doing business together.

Trump tells the same kind of story about himself: he does everything wrong in real estate, digs in the wrong spot, and somehow still finds the gold mine underneath it.

Luck isn't random. It's a frequency you can learn to carry.

Larry King asked Bill Gates, live, on national television: what's the secret to your success?

He didn't say hard work. He didn't say intelligence. He said he was at the right place at the right time, and luck had a lot to do with it. Most successful people say the same thing behind closed doors — they just don't say it on camera.

But there's a second half to what he said that almost nobody repeats: there were plenty of other people standing in that exact same lucky spot. The difference was vision. He could see what the opportunity actually was.

Luck opens the door. Vision is what lets you walk through it.

A stranger in a hotel bar in 1979 taught Kevin something that took decades to fully understand.

He was a young guy trying to make it, and asked an older, wealthy businessman the secret to success. The man picked up a box of matches and said: imagine this is an acorn. What do you see?

Kevin said a tree. The man said that was good — but when he looked at the same acorn, he saw a forest. One acorn, a tree, and every tree that tree could ever grow.

That's depth of vision. Most people are still looking at the matchbox.

If you cook someone a beautiful meal and they barely touch it, you don't cook for them again.

The universe works exactly the same way. It wants to give you what you want — but if you're handed an opportunity and you don't actually take it, don't appreciate it, don't use it, it stops showing up. Taste it, love it, and the universe starts cooking you twice as much.

What you want wants you back. Kevin says it isn't a metaphor — it's the actual mechanism behind what people call luck.
